lessonTitle: Sexually Transmitted Infection and Sexual Health

blocks.text: A 20-year-old returns a postal chlamydia screening kit and is told the result is positive. She has no symptoms and no idea who gave it to her. Her current partner says he feels perfectly well and sees no reason to be treated. Over the next ten minutes you will have to take a non-judgemental sexual history, choose a treatment, and persuade people to be tested without breaking confidentiality. That is the core skill of this unit.

blocks.markdown:
**Taking a sexual history.** Many patients are embarrassed, so create the conditions for honesty: a private room, an explanation of why you are asking, assurance of **confidentiality** and its limits, neutral open questions and inclusive language that does not assume gender or orientation. A structured approach, often called the **five Ps**, covers:

- **Partners**: number and gender in recent months, new or casual partners, partner symptoms.
- **Practices**: types of sex (vaginal, anal, oral) so that the correct anatomical sites are tested.
- **Protection** from STI (condom use) and from pregnancy.
- **Past STI** history and prior testing, including HIV and hepatitis status.
- **Prevention**: vaccination (hepatitis B, HPV), HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), cervical screening.

Also ask about the date of last unprotected sex (relevant to emergency contraception, post-exposure prophylaxis and test timing), symptoms (discharge, dysuria, ulcers, pelvic pain, rash), drug use and sex under the influence (chemsex), sexual violence and coercion, and age-related safeguarding concerns. **Risk assessment** identifies who needs a full screen: a new partner or more than one partner in the last year, inconsistent condom use, partner with an STI, age under 25, sex worker or partner from a high-prevalence area.

rows: Often asymptomatic (most women); discharge, dysuria, intermenstrual bleeding, pelvic pain
NAAT on vulvovaginal swab (women) or first-catch urine (men)
Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days (azithromycin if doxycycline unsuitable)
Discharge, dysuria; often asymptomatic in women; can cause PID, Bartholin abscess, disseminated infection
NAAT plus culture before treatment for antibiotic sensitivities
Primary: painless ulcer (chancre) with painless lymph nodes; secondary: rash incl. palms and soles, condylomata lata, mucous patches; latent; tertiary: gumma, cardiovascular and neurosyphilis
Treponemal antibody EIA confirmed by a second treponemal test; non-treponemal test (RPR/VDRL) to monitor activity
Benzathine benzylpenicillin 2.4 million units intramuscularly for early syphilis
blocks.caption: Drug regimens are teaching examples; check against current BASHH and local guidance.

blocks.markdown:
**Chlamydia and gonorrhoea.** Both infect the cervix and urethra and can ascend to cause PID with tubal scarring, ectopic pregnancy and infertility. Because most infections are asymptomatic, screening of sexually active young women is a public health strategy. In pregnancy, they can cause neonatal conjunctivitis and pneumonia (chlamydia) and ophthalmia neonatorum (gonorrhoea). Test at all exposed sites (throat and rectum as indicated by sexual practices), treat, advise abstinence until treatment and partners are treated, and test for other STIs including HIV and syphilis. Repeat testing at about three months detects reinfection. Gonorrhoea antibiotic resistance is increasing, so culture allows sensitivity testing and a test of cure is advised.

**Syphilis.** Primary infection follows an incubation of about 3 weeks; the chancre heals spontaneously, which falsely reassures. Secondary syphilis (weeks to months later) is a systemic illness with a non-itchy rash including the palms and soles. **Early latent** infection is asymptomatic and found on serology; **tertiary** disease occurs years later. Syphilis in pregnancy can cause congenital syphilis, so antenatal screening is routine. Following treatment, the non-treponemal titre should fall at least four-fold (two doubling dilutions) in 6 to 12 months. A **Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction** (fever, headache, myalgia within hours of the first penicillin dose due to the release of bacterial antigens) is common and self-limiting.

blocks.title: Risk assessment and testing after a new partner
blocks.prompt: A 22-year-old woman presents with intermenstrual spotting. She had unprotected vaginal and oral sex with a new male partner 5 weeks ago, and condoms are used inconsistently. She has no ulcers or pelvic pain. Her pregnancy test is negative. Determine the tests and the key counselling points.

steps.text: Risk assessment: a new partner, inconsistent condom use and age under 25 mark her as higher risk. Intermenstrual bleeding is a common presentation of chlamydial cervicitis, though many women are asymptomatic.

Select tests by exposure: vulvovaginal NAAT for chlamydia and gonorrhoea (plus a pharyngeal swab for oral sex, if indicated); blood tests for HIV and syphilis, with a combined antigen and antibody HIV test; consider hepatitis B immunity. The window period of tests means that repeat testing may be needed if exposure was recent.

Counsel: results pathway and confidentiality; treat promptly if positive; avoid sex until she and her partner are treated; discuss condoms and contraception; arrange partner notification and offer HPV and hepatitis B vaccination where appropriate.

blocks.answer: Vulvovaginal NAAT for chlamydia and gonorrhoea, blood tests for HIV and syphilis (offer hepatitis B), counselling on confidentiality, abstinence, partner notification and prevention.

blocks.markdown:
**Partner notification (contact tracing)** aims to treat infected partners, prevent reinfection of the index patient and interrupt transmission. The **look-back period** is the time before diagnosis during which partners should be contacted; it depends on the infection and symptoms (for example, about 6 months or the most recent partner for chlamydia in asymptomatic infection) and is set by BASHH guidance. Methods are **patient referral** (the patient informs partners, with support such as a letter or text), **provider referral** (the clinic contacts partners anonymously, without naming the index patient) and **contingent referral** (provider contacts partners if the patient has not done so within an agreed time). Partners are offered testing and may be treated empirically before results.

**Confidentiality.** Sexual health services are confidential, and information is not shared with the GP or family without consent. The duty is not absolute: disclosure without consent may be justified when it is necessary to protect others from serious harm, for example a partner at risk of HIV where the patient refuses to inform them, after discussing and documenting the reasons and informing the patient where possible. A young person under 16 may be competent to consent to sexual health care (Gillick competence), and clinicians must assess **safeguarding** concerns such as coercion, exploitation, a large age gap or abuse.

blocks.title: Planning partner notification after a gonorrhoea diagnosis
blocks.prompt: A 26-year-old woman is diagnosed with gonorrhoea. She had one regular partner in the past 3 months and one casual partner 6 weeks ago. She is anxious about her regular partner finding out about the casual partner. Outline a plan that protects her privacy and prevents reinfection.

steps.text: Define who to notify: both partners fall within the look-back period for gonorrhoea (about 3 months for asymptomatic infection, longer for some situations; follow BASHH guidance). Both need testing and presumptive treatment.

Choose the method: offer provider referral so that the clinic can notify each partner without disclosing her identity or the other partner's existence, or contingent referral if she prefers to tell them herself.

Prevent reinfection and complications: advise avoiding sex until she and her partners have completed treatment, arrange test of cure with culture, repeat screening at 3 months, and complete screening for HIV and syphilis. Document discussions and the agreed plan.

blocks.answer: Use provider (or contingent) referral for both partners within the look-back period, with abstinence until treated, test of cure and re-screening, while maintaining her confidentiality.

items: Take a non-judgemental history, tailored to practices, to determine which sites and tests are needed.
Most chlamydial and gonococcal infections in women are asymptomatic; test and treat to prevent PID and infertility.
Syphilis passes through primary, secondary, latent and tertiary stages and is monitored by non-treponemal titres.
Partner notification is part of treatment, not an optional extra.
Confidentiality is the default; breaches require justification and, where possible, the patient's knowledge.

blocks.title: Treat the pair, not the patient
blocks.text: A patient treated for an STI is reinfected if an untreated partner continues to have sex with them. Partner notification, abstinence until treatment is complete and repeat testing form part of the treatment plan.

blocks.title: Test the sites that were exposed
blocks.text: Choose swabs by sexual practice: vulvovaginal or urethral for genital exposure, pharyngeal for oral sex and rectal for receptive anal sex. A genital-only test misses infection at other sites, and gonorrhoea and chlamydia are frequently asymptomatic there.

points: A structured, non-judgemental sexual history (partners, practices, protection, past STI, prevention) drives risk assessment and test selection.
Chlamydia is often asymptomatic and diagnosed by NAAT; gonorrhoea needs NAAT and culture; syphilis is staged clinically and monitored by serology.
Partner notification uses patient, provider or contingent referral within a defined look-back period.
Confidentiality is central to sexual health care and may be breached only exceptionally to prevent serious harm.

questions.stem: Which approach is most appropriate when starting a sexual history with a young patient?

options.text: Explain why you are asking, reassure about confidentiality and its limits, and use open, non-judgemental questions without assuming gender or orientation
Ask the patient's parent to answer the questions for accuracy
Begin with questions about the number of lifetime partners to assess promiscuity
Avoid asking about sexual practices unless the patient mentions symptoms

questions.correctOptionText: Explain why you are asking, reassure about confidentiality and its limits, and use open, non-judgemental questions without assuming gender or orientation

distractorRationale.a: Correct: trust and clarity enable honest disclosure.
distractorRationale.b: Involving a parent without consent breaches confidentiality and discourages honesty.
distractorRationale.c: Judgemental framing damages rapport; the aim is risk assessment, not moral judgement.
distractorRationale.d: Omitting practices would miss infections at throat and rectal sites and silent infections.

questions.explanation: Patients disclose more when they understand why questions are asked and trust that information is confidential. Inclusive, open questions also ensure that the right anatomical sites are tested.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman has no symptoms but had unprotected vaginal sex with a new partner 6 weeks ago. Which set of tests is most appropriate?

options.text: Vulvovaginal NAAT for chlamydia and gonorrhoea, plus blood tests for HIV and syphilis
Chlamydia test only, since she has no symptoms
No tests, since symptoms are required before testing
Blood cultures and a pelvic MRI

questions.correctOptionText: Vulvovaginal NAAT for chlamydia and gonorrhoea, plus blood tests for HIV and syphilis

distractorRationale.a: Correct: a new partner and unprotected sex warrant a full screen, with repeat testing if within a window period.
distractorRationale.b: A single test misses gonorrhoea, HIV and syphilis.
distractorRationale.c: Most STIs are asymptomatic, so symptoms are not required.
distractorRationale.d: Blood cultures and MRI have no role in screening.

questions.explanation: Risk assessment identifies a new unprotected exposure, so a full screen is indicated even without symptoms. Window periods for some tests mean that repeat testing may be needed later.

questions.stem: Which is the preferred sample for diagnosing genital chlamydia infection in a woman?

options.text: Self-taken vulvovaginal swab for nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT)
Culture on blood agar
Gram stain of a vaginal swab
Serum IgG antibody

questions.correctOptionText: Self-taken vulvovaginal swab for nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT)

distractorRationale.a: Correct: NAAT on a vulvovaginal swab is the most sensitive and acceptable test.
distractorRationale.b: Chlamydia is an obligate intracellular organism and does not grow on routine culture media.
distractorRationale.c: Gram stain does not identify chlamydia.
distractorRationale.d: Serology cannot distinguish current from past infection.

questions.explanation: Chlamydia trachomatis is an obligate intracellular bacterium, so NAAT detecting its nucleic acid is the diagnostic method of choice. A self-taken vulvovaginal swab is as sensitive as a clinician-taken endocervical swab.

questions.stem: A woman has a mucopurulent cervical discharge. A Gram stain shows Gram-negative intracellular diplococci. Which statement about further management is correct?

options.text: Take a culture before treatment for antibiotic sensitivity, treat with ceftriaxone, and arrange partner notification and test of cure
Treat with a single dose of benzathine benzylpenicillin
No further tests are needed because the Gram stain is conclusive and resistance does not occur
Treat with antifungals

questions.correctOptionText: Take a culture before treatment for antibiotic sensitivity, treat with ceftriaxone, and arrange partner notification and test of cure

distractorRationale.a: Correct: culture gives antibiotic susceptibility because resistance is increasing; ceftriaxone is first-line and a test of cure is advised.
distractorRationale.b: Benzathine benzylpenicillin is used for syphilis, not gonorrhoea.
distractorRationale.c: Gonococcal resistance is increasing, so culture and sensitivity testing matter.
distractorRationale.d: The organism is bacterial; antifungals are irrelevant.

questions.explanation: Gram-negative intracellular diplococci indicate Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Because antimicrobial resistance is an increasing problem, culture is obtained before treatment and a test of cure confirms eradication (check BASHH guidance).

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman has a generalised non-itchy rash involving her palms and soles, generalised lymphadenopathy and painless white mucosal patches in the mouth. Which diagnosis and investigation are most appropriate?

options.text: Secondary syphilis; treponemal serology with a non-treponemal titre
Primary syphilis; dark-field microscopy only
Gonorrhoea; urethral swab culture
Chlamydia; NAAT of first-catch urine

questions.correctOptionText: Secondary syphilis; treponemal serology with a non-treponemal titre

distractorRationale.a: Correct: rash on palms and soles, lymphadenopathy and mucous patches are the features of secondary syphilis, confirmed by serology.
distractorRationale.b: Primary syphilis presents with a painless chancre, not a generalised rash.
distractorRationale.c: Gonorrhoea does not cause this rash.
distractorRationale.d: Chlamydia does not produce this systemic syndrome.

questions.explanation: Secondary syphilis is a spirochaetal bacteraemic phase producing a widespread non-itchy rash that includes the palms and soles, with lymphadenopathy and mucous patches. Serology (treponemal tests with a non-treponemal titre to monitor response) is positive at this stage.

questions.stem: Before treatment for early syphilis, a patient's RPR titre is 1:64. Six months after treatment it is 1:8. By what factor has the titre fallen (fold decrease)?
questions.explanation: Fold decrease = 64 / 8 = 8, which corresponds to three doubling dilutions (64, 32, 16, 8). A decline of at least four-fold (two dilutions) at 6 to 12 months indicates an adequate response, so this patient has responded well.

questions.stem: A clinic offers chlamydia screening to 1,500 asymptomatic women aged 18 to 24 years. The prevalence of infection is 8% and the NAAT sensitivity is 95%. How many infected women are expected to test positive?
questions.explanation: Infected women = 1,500 x 0.08 = 120. With 95% sensitivity, expected true positives = 120 x 0.95 = 114, and about 6 infected women are missed. This yield justifies screening a young, high-prevalence group because each detected case can be treated to prevent PID and infertility.

questions.stem: True or false: a clinician's duty of confidentiality in sexual health is absolute, so a patient's diagnosis may never be disclosed to anyone without consent in any circumstances.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Confidentiality is the strong default, but disclosure without consent may be justified in exceptional circumstances, such as protecting a partner from serious harm when the patient has refused to inform them. Any disclosure should be limited, documented and, where possible, discussed with the patient first.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old is diagnosed with chlamydia. She asks that her parents are not told and says she has had two partners in the last 4 months, one of whom is 29 years old. Discuss how you would handle consent, confidentiality, partner notification and safeguarding.
markingGuide: Assess capacity and understanding (Gillick competence); a competent young person can consent to sexual health care
Maintain confidentiality, not informing parents without consent, unless there is serious risk of harm
Explain the limits of confidentiality and document the discussion
Safeguarding: assess for coercion, exploitation, abuse and age difference; follow local safeguarding procedures, which may require disclosure
Partner notification: identify partners in the look-back period; options patient, provider or contingent referral; offer testing and treatment
Abstain from sex until treatment complete, repeat test at 3 months, screen for other STIs including HIV and syphilis
questions.explanation: A competent young person keeps the right to confidential care, but the age difference with a 29-year-old partner raises safeguarding concerns, which may justify sharing information with appropriate agencies. Partner notification prevents reinfection and further spread.

questions.stem: Compare the presentation, diagnostic testing and example treatment of chlamydia, gonorrhoea and syphilis, and explain why untreated chlamydia and gonorrhoea matter in women.
markingGuide: Chlamydia: often asymptomatic; discharge, dysuria, intermenstrual bleeding; NAAT; doxycycline or alternative
Gonorrhoea: discharge, dysuria, often asymptomatic in women; NAAT plus culture for sensitivities; ceftriaxone; test of cure
Syphilis: primary chancre, secondary rash including palms and soles, latent and tertiary stages; treponemal serology and non-treponemal titres; benzathine benzylpenicillin
Complications of untreated chlamydia and gonorrhoea: PID, tubal damage, ectopic pregnancy, infertility, chronic pelvic pain, neonatal infection
Regimens are teaching examples; check against current BASHH and local guidance
questions.explanation: Each infection has a characteristic presentation and test, and treatment is organism-specific. Chlamydia and gonorrhoea are mainly asymptomatic in women, so screening and early treatment prevent PID and its sequelae.
